title: How to Set Up a Multi-Camera Home Security System From Scratch
excerpt: Sketch entries, power, Wi-Fi, and storage before you buy anything: a from-scratch full multi-camera layout that avoids blind spots and rework.
author: HiddenCameras Editorial Team
authorBio: The HiddenCameras.tv editorial team researches and writes about security cameras, surveillance technology, and home safety.
body:
Do not buy a single camera until you have walked your property with a notebook. Multi-camera systems fail in the shopping cart, not on the wall: people buy four identical cameras, mount them where drilling is easy, and discover later that the side gate and the darkest corner of the driveway sit in blind spots. An hour of planning on paper saves you from owning the wrong cameras in the wrong places.

This guide builds your system in professional order: map the property, count entries, sort out power and Wi-Fi, then buy cameras that fit the map. Follow it once and every camera you add later slots into a plan.

Walk your property with a notebook before buying anything

Start at the street and walk to your front door the way a stranger would, noting every path to any door or ground-floor window: the main walk, the driveway, the side gate, the gap between garage and fence. Repeat after dark, because bushes, fences, and parked cars cast different shadows at night. Each route you trace is a corridor your cameras must collectively watch.

Repeat indoors, tracing the path from each exterior door to the bedrooms. The hallways those paths share are your indoor choke points. Most homes have two or three outdoor corridors and one or two indoor ones, which is why finished systems land at three to five cameras rather than the eight-packs people assume they need.

Count entries, not rooms

Beginners assign one camera per room; experienced installers assign cameras to entries, because a camera on a door documents everyone who passes while one in a spare bedroom documents nothing for months. List every exterior door and ground-floor window hidden from the street. Secluded ones get priority, since seclusion is what intruders select for.

Give the main approach two overlapping views

Sketch overlapping views so each entry sits inside at least one camera's cone and the main approach sits inside two. Overlap is deliberate redundancy for blocked views. For ideas once your sketch is done, see where to mount cameras around your home.

One brand or a mix: the tradeoff nobody mentions

A single brand means one app, one alert style, and one timeline to reconstruct at midnight when something happens. If fast review matters more than perfect specs, standardize on one ecosystem and accept that its weakest camera still beats a stronger one whose app you never open.

A mixed system picks the best tool per position: wired for the driveway, discreet for the hallway, battery for the outlet-less shed. The price is complexity across apps, storage, and alerts. Mix only when a position demands something your main brand cannot do, and keep the odd unit to a single camera.

Power and Wi-Fi are the real system; cameras are accessories

For each planned position, record two facts: where its power comes from, and how strong the Wi-Fi is at that exact spot, measured with your phone held where the lens will sit. A camera with a perfect view and one bar of signal records slideshow stills.

Spend battery cameras only on unreachable spots

Prefer wired power wherever cable hides along eaves or baseboards, since continuous power unlocks continuous recording. Reserve battery cameras for genuinely unreachable spots and accept their limits: shorter clips, cooldown gaps, and recharging chores. Fix weak Wi-Fi now, by moving the router or shifting the camera position, not after mounting.

Name your cameras like street signs, not gadgets

Label each camera by what it watches and which way it faces: Front Door Facing Street, Driveway Facing Garage, Hallway Facing Bedrooms. When an alert fires, the name tells you what is happening before video loads, and anyone in the household can find footage without a guided tour.

Keep the same discipline in settings: one time zone, one clip length, and saved files dated first. Future you, exporting footage for a report or claim, needs files that sort themselves.

Decide how many days of history you actually need

Storage is a question about habits. Daily reviewers need only a few days of rolling history, since anything important gets saved to a phone the same day. Frequent travelers and remote landlords need longer retention so a late discovery is still on disk. Match cards, hubs, or cloud plans to that answer instead of buying the largest option by default.

Whatever you choose, build one habit that beats capacity: save important clips off the camera the day they happen. Cameras get stolen and rolling storage overwrites; a clip in your phone gallery survives both.

The first-week tuning pass most people skip

Treat the first week as a draft, with every false alert a work order. Cars triggering the driveway camera mean the zone includes the street and must shrink. Moths swarming the porch camera mean its light attracts insects and the mount must shift. One camera spamming while others stay quiet means its sensitivity needs matching to its siblings.

End the week with a drill: walk every corridor after dark while someone watches alerts arrive. Confirm each walk produced a prompt notification and a recognizable face, not a silhouette. Anything failing gets re-aimed or reconfigured while the ladder is still out.
